A hill named after George Henry Brown, a businessman who arrived in Singapore in the 1840s. Covering 223 hectares, the area is recognised for its considerable ecological and biodiversity value. It was originally the property of George Henry Brown before being converted into the Bukit Brown Rubber Estate. The site was subsequently acquired by three Hokkien entrepreneurs, Ong Kew Ho, Ong Ewe Hai and Ong Chong Chew and turned into a burial ground known as Seh Ong Cemetery. Between 1922 and 1973, it became the site of the Bukit Brown Municipal Cemetery after section of the Seh Ong Cemetery was acquired by the municipal government.

Geographical region that stretched from Geylang Serai to Upper Serangoon Road, and was bounded by Paya Lebar Road, Upper Serangoon Road, Changi Road and Bedok Reservoir, encompassing areas that included the former Kampong Melayu and present day Tai Seng. The region, which means “lemongrass farm” in Teochew, was originally part of the Perseverance Estate owned by the European settler and landowner, Jose d’Almeida before it was converted into lemongrass plantations. Village located within present-day Yishun New Town (former Nee Soon estate), stretching from Sembawang Road to Sungei Khatib Bongsu. It was originally named Chong Pang Village in 1938, which was then located opposite Sembawang Aerodrome at the 12th milestone, before renamed Chye Kay Village in 1954, after Tan Chye Kay, a Chinese pioneer and community leader who owned rubber and pineapple plantations in the area. Landmarks in the village included the Chu Sion Tong Temple, Lee Cheng School and Kwang Teck School (both schools were constructed in the 1930s). The main economic activities of the villagers included vegetable farming, fishing and orchid farming. In the 1980s, the village was evacuated as a result of urbanisation. Part of the plantations of Chye Kay Village is occupied by the present day Yishun Park. The location of the village is presently marked by the Chye Kay Village Heritage Garden at Block 264 Yishun Street 22.

It became a residential neighbourhood in the early 1900s and was occupied by Peranakan families by the 1930s. Singapore Chinese Girls' School was once located here.

In 1991, the entire area was redeveloped and is now called Esplanade Park.

Located along Connaught Drive, opposite the Padang and City Hall, it is one of Singapore's oldest heritage parks, built in 1943. Queen Elizabeth Walk, the promenade at the sea-front, was opened on 30 May 1953. At that time, the rest of the area, including the Esplanade Gardens, was named the Singapore Esplanade. Heritage site that was originally the Serangoon Road Racecourse belonging to the Singapore Sporting Club, the predecessor of the Singapore Turf Club. In 1935, two years after the Turf Club moved to Bukit Timah, it was re-named Farrer Park after R. J. Farrer, president of the Municipal Commissioners (1919-1931). Farrer Park housed sports fields, a stadium with athletic track and a Sports House during the sixties and seventies. Later, part of the site was used for a school and a housing development, leaving only an open field. It was marked a historic site on 6 Apr 2003. The public sports field is presently known as Farrer Park Field.

One of the first Christian burial grounds in Singapore that comprised two burial sites located on Fort Canning Hill. One was located near the hilltop close to the bungalow built by Stamford Raffles which was in use between 1819 and 1822. The second burial site, located on the slopes of Fort Canning Hill, was in use between 1822 and 1865. The cemetery was extended, with a brick wall and a pair of gates of Gothic design added to the cemetery in 1846. In the 1970s, with the establishment of Fort Canning Park, the graves in the cemetery were exhumed. The site of the cemetery is now known as Fort Canning Green.

Located in the eastern part of Singapore, this predominantly Malay precinct is one of the oldest Malay Settlements and is reputed as the Malay emporium of Singapore. Lemon grass, known as serai in Malay, was extensively cultivated and grown here in the later half of the 19th century, hence the name of the area. It was formerly part of the Perseverance Estate owned by Alsagoff and Company. During the Japanese Occupation, the people here started planting tapioca. The first three blocks of flats in the area were built in 1965 under the Geylang Serai Housing Scheme. The area saw the completion of HDB flats, Industrial Estates of light industries and shopping complexes by the early 1980s. The Malay Village was set up in the area to preserve the Malay cultural heritage. It showcased a replica of a Malay kampung and promoted traditional Malay handicraft and activities.

Former barracks that house leading international and home-grown galleries, national research centre NTU Centre for Contemporary Art (CCA) Singapore, and art organisations such as Art Outreach and Playeum’s Children’s Centre for Creativity. The barracks, located at Lock Road off Alexandra Road, was originally built to accommodate the 1st Battalion, the Middlesex Regiment of the British army. It was named after General Sir Webb Gillman, a British army officer. It was handed over to the Singapore government in August 1971 and was known as Gillman Camp when the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) moved in. It was renamed Gillman Village in 1996 and the buildings were opened to the public for commercial use after the SAF vacated the camp. In 2010, it reverted to its original name of Gillman Barracks and was officially launched as an art district on 15 September 2012. Part of the Gillman Barracks is presently occupied by the condominium, The Interface.

Petain Road and Tyrwhitt Road Conservation Area

Conservation area located outside the boundaries of the Little India Conservation Area. The original conservation area, which was gazetted on 25 October 1991, stretches along Jalan Besar Road and Foch Road, the upper portions of Tessensohn Road, Race Course Road and Tyrwhitt Road, along Cavan Road and Hamilton Road, a stretch of Owen Road, parts of Kitchener Road, Sam Leong Road, Maude Road, Desker Road and Rowell Road. It also includes the ornate rows of terrace houses along Petain Road and a short stretch of Syed Alwi Road. Subsequently, other buildings in the area were given conservation status over the years, including shophouses along Jellicoe Road, Lavender Street and Serangoon Road; a 4-storey Art Deco style building at 27 Maude Road; the former Victoria School; shophouses at Roberts Lane, Birch Road and Townshend Road, as well as the Mahatma Gandhi Memorial Hall.

An area in the western part of Singapore which was a mangrove swamp before it was developed into an industrial estate in 1961. The boundaries of Jurong have shifted over time. It was originally a small piece of land between Peng Kang (present day Jurong West and Boon Lay) and Bukit Timah, roughly where Bukit Batok is today. In a map dated to 1911, the Jurong area was bounded by Jurong Road in the south, Choa Chu Kang in the north and west, and Bukit Timah Road in the east. It was a broader region spanning Pandan and Peng Kang in the south and reached Tuas in the west in the memory of some people. The area has since transformed into a self-sufficient town consisting of five administrative zones, with residential areas and recreational amenities.

An island located 5.6 km south-west of Singapore. The island, originally made up of two small coral outtcrop, was first known in the 17th century as Governor's Island. During the colonial period, it served as the burial site for immigrants who died in quarantine on Lazarus and St John's Islands, and was the site of a signal station. A Chinese temple dedicated to the deity Tua Pek Kong and three Malay keramat on the island is the centre of worship for pilgrims who visited the island between September and October.

Nature reserve bordered by Port Road and Labrador Villa Road off Pasir Panjang Road. It was designated as a nature reserve (since 1951), then degazetted as a nature park (since 1973) before being gazetted as a nature reserve again in 2002. Fort Pasir Panjang and the Labrador Battery is located within the nature reserve.

Singapore's first civil and only large prison facility before the contruction of Changi Prison in 1936. Built in 1847, the civil jail was then known as H. M. Jail or H. M. Prison. Extension to the civil jail was added between 1879 and 1882, with Her Majesty’s Service Criminal Jail built next to it in 1882. The whole prison complex was collectively known as Outram Prison. After World War II, the headquarters of the newly established Prisons Department was housed in the administrative block within the prison complex. Beginning in 1963, the prison was demolished to make way for the construction of the Outram Park Estate. The site of the prison complex near Outram MRT Station has been marked as a historic site by National Heritage Board.

Military installation. It was the site of the largest British Royal Air Force (RAF) base in the Far East that became operational in 1928. An island located south of Singapore. It was previously known as Pulau Blakang Mati between 1830 and 1972, and Pulau Panjang before that. During the early colonial period, several villages inhabited by the Bugis, Malay and Chinese existed on the island. From 1880s onwards, the British used the island as a military base with the construction of Fort Serapong, Fort Connaught, Fort Siloso and the Mount Imbiah Battery. After the British withdrawal in 1967, the Singapore Naval Volunteer Force was relocated to the island. It was renamed Sentosa in 1970 and developed into a resort island administered by the Sentosa Development Corporation in 1972. Attractions such as Fort Siloso, Butterfly Park and the Underwater World Singapore were developed over the years. In 2003, the waterfront residences, Sentosa Cove was launched, followed by the opening of the first integrated resort in Singapore, Resorts World Sentosa in 2010. The island's Capella Hotel was also the site of the historic summit between the President of the United States, Donald Trump, and North Korean leader, Kim Jong Un, on 12 Jun 2018.

Flea market that existed along Sungei Road between Jalan Besar and Rochor Canal Road. It began as a small trading spot along the river in the 1930s, operating between 3 and 6pm. It was nicknamed "Robinson Petang", meaning "evening Robinson", a cheeky reference to the Robinsons department store except it was for the poor man. After the Japanese Occupation, it became known as the Thieves Market from its reputation as a place where stolen, smuggled or illegal goods were peddled. It later became the place to trade second-hand and vintage goods. The market's popularity waned from the 1980s and it was eventually closed in 2017.

Related Descriptor: Amusement park located at the seventh milestone along Upper Bukit Timah Road, bounded by Chun Tin Road and Jalan Jurong Kechil. The name of the amusement park means “Greater East Asia World” in Cantonese, a reference to Imperial Japan’s concept of the Greater East Asia Co- Prosperity Sphere during World War II. Attractions in the amusement park include stages for wayang and getai, a dance hall, coffee parlours, a cinema that screened Japanese and old Chinese films, food stalls and a gambling hall. It was converted into the Beauty World Market in 1947.

It was known as the 'Street of Krishnan Temple' by the Tamils as the Sri Krishnan Temple is located here. The street is lined with religious buildings and arts organisations, including the Kwan Im Thong Hood Cho Temple and Stamford Arts Centre. Older generation Hokkiens referred to this street as 'Si Beh Lor', which literally means 'Four Horse Road'.
